rules.rule: Plain natural read; never slowed or over-directed; stress at most 1 word per 3-4 sentences
Characters front-facing only (the approved HD cast); no side or 3/4 views
Zero visual glitches: no flicker, torn text or jumps between frames
Every video argues one clear thesis with our own calculation or comparison; never a reworded article
Open on the mystery or stake in the first 15 s; never a channel greeting
About 70% evergreen (explainers, lists, guides, comparisons, case studies), 30% trending; news reactions kept rare
One big emotional subject, 2-4 huge words that add tension (never repeat the title), readable at phone size
No background music; voice plus light SFX, final mix -14 LUFS
Numbers read off a chart are labelled approximate on screen; plot only sourced points, never invented in-between values
All on-screen text must read on a phone: slide body text 30 px+, no tiny caps sub-lines
No shot holds still for more than ~5 s; add a build, a prop or a cut
Show our own maths exactly as in facts.json (same inputs, same rounding)
Illustrate what the voice says: every sentence gets at least one visual that depicts its words (a vignette, an object, a scene action) — pose changes and generic icons do not count
Characters act inside scenes (sit, hold, interact, two-person moments) instead of standing beside them; props rest on surfaces or in hands, never float; frames as bright as the Alux reference (~15%)
At most ~3 keyword slams per video, saved for the real payoff lines
Show every line as a visual metaphor or a small object story (house of cards, money mountain, bank on balloons); text slides only for the key numbers (aim ≤ 25% of runtime)
Crowds of small characters on round pedestals holding coin stacks to show who owns what; split-screen grids (4–6 panels) and circles for lists and comparisons
Continuous transitions: zoom into an object and it becomes the next scene — avoid plain cuts
Keep CapitalCode's own dark navy + champagne brand (owner, 2026-10-24): adopt Kurzgesagt's editing, never its pastel look

rules.rule: Illustrate almost every word: a new visual element every ~1 s (2–3 spoken words). Measured: Kurzgesagt one change every 0.8 s, our first video every 4.8 s
Shorts 1-3 (2026-10-25) are the quality floor: no video may look worse; every new video must aim for better-looking illustrations than the last.
Every illustration is in sync with the voiceover: what is said is shown at that moment, landing on its word, never early or late.
Draw a specific, good-looking illustration for what each line actually says — not a generic picture that only roughly fits.

Every script must make complete sense: each sentence follows logically from the one before, every claim and number is explained, no jumps, gaps or vague lines. Read it aloud start to finish as a viewer before voicing.

Zero wrong information: every number comes from a real source in facts.json, and every finance concept (how index funds, interest, inflation, markets etc. work) is explained correctly and checked against a reputable source before voicing. If unsure, cut it or rewrite it until it is certainly true; never simplify into something false.
Clean layout: no text may ever overlap other text or art, including during transitions and crossfades; every label has its own clear space.

Nothing appears before it is spoken: a name, number or item shows in the caption and the illustration only when the voice says it — never ahead, especially in fast lists of names. Check list timings against the actual audio.

Every video passes a line-by-line accuracy audit before voicing (audit.json, gate-enforced): each sentence checked against its source and for logical sense, every own calculation re-done independently, and the headline result reality-checked against an outside source.

Make every video noticeably more alive: the HD cast acts out the key story beats (signing, paying, counting, reading a bill, reacting, running, celebrating) with the acting pose library and props in hand, synced word by word; objects-only scenes and tiny static pedestal figures are not enough

When a big total is made of many small payments (fees, interest, cuts), say the per-transaction amount first (e.g. about 1.7 cents per dollar) and then what it added up to over the year; never state a yearly total so it sounds like one payment, and never credit a total to only part of its source
When writing a script, make sure it is all correct, makes sense and is easy to understand for viewers
Make everything right the first time (script, drawings, illustrations, text, layout); we cannot fix and re-render again and again

Pick topics viewers can't help clicking: a surprising, personal stake (their money, a thing they use daily, a hidden cost or trick) proven by outlier videos at 2x+ channel median; never a dry or textbook subject
Shorts need one-idea topics (one object, one number, one twist, e.g. why prices end in .99); bigger how-it-works system stories are long-form material

Every Short gets 3 drawn covers (ThumbShort): sticker title top third with ONE large key word, a stake object cut from the Short's own art in the middle, a cast close-up with a clear expression at the bottom, plain saturated background — never a raw video frame.

Every hook (long + Shorts) must feel PERSONAL, Alux-style, ~25-30 s, brand sting only AFTER the hook. Use all 7: (1) first word is about the viewer ("You..."), not the topic; (2) friend tone ("You know...", "okay?"); (3) tie the fact to the viewer's own life; (4) answer their doubt before they have it ("you don't need to be a billionaire to..."); (5) put them inside the story ("Imagine you're..."); (6) small everyday details and numbers; (7) say their next thought out loud ("Now you're thinking..."). Then promise the full range (small to huge) and the steps/levels the video walks through. Facts stay sourced and exact; copy structure only, never Alux art or lines. EXAMPLE (trusts video) - BAD (topic-first): a casino billionaire, $7.9 billion, a $2.8 billion tax bill. GOOD (personal): "When you die, the government can take up to 40% of what you leave your kids. You'd probably expect billionaires to pay the most. But one casino owner handed his family $7.9 billion and dodged a $2.8 billion tax bill, legally. And you don't need to be a billionaire to understand how. Today, we'll break down the three steps they use, one by one."

Pick the structure that fits the topic: a story-driven flow (topics grow out of what just happened) OR a clear list of lessons/steps when the topic suits it (rules, mistakes, steps).
